rv.q: A superb all-male ensemble, under the powerhouse direction of Kenny Leon, attacks this knock-your-socks-off drama with intense emotional passion and intellectual courage.
“A Soldier’s Play’ remains a strikingly taut drama that you don’t want to end.

Even in a Broadway landscape that could give home to the explosive Slave Play, Fuller’s 1981 mystery remains a bracing slap of a drama, a thoughtful examination of American bigotry and the many tolls it exacts.
The production, directed by Kenny Leon, brings Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning play roaring back to life with a cast that understands both the text's anger and its compassion.
Leon’s muscular production makes a solid case for the play, if not as a top-tier classic then at the very least as a stirring indictment of the cancer of racism.
Charles Fuller's 1981. Pulitzer Prize-winning drama about racial tensions in a segregated Army base during World War II receives a powerful revival that feels urgently relevant to our current moment.
His performance has size and precision, monstrosity and humanity.
Like the bare wood of Derek McLane’s set, it gets the job done, and it provides a platform for powerful moments and performances.
A magnetic Underwood holds the proceedings together smartly.
Despite some powerful acting, it is too distracted to make the case.
After some 40 years, “A Soldier’s Play” still hits home, summoning a world at war with itself.

It is a fiercely written and directed (by Kenny Leon), and beautifully performed, indictment of cultural and institutional racism, and not just the damage racists do with their words and fists but the damage racism does to the minds of black people.
A Soldier’s Play is worth the sprint.
Through and through, this is an exceedingly well-thought-out and riveting production.

Notwithstanding the value of this play's dramatized vision of life for black enlistees before President Truman signed an executive order in 1948 ending segregation in the armed services, it is the play's character-driven plot that keeps us in its thrall from start to finish.
The raw truth is exposed for society to see past injustices in a teachable piece evoking somber reflection.

Charles Fuller's murder mystery, finally on Broadway in a fine production directed by Kenny Leon some four decades after it won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, is so good that even if you've seen the 1984 movie adaptation and remember who done it, the play is still riveting.
A Fantastic 'Soldier's Play' on About More Than Just Blair Underwood's Pecs: Underwood stars alongside David Alan Grier and Jerry O'Connell in a landmark Pulitzer winner making its Broadway debut.
Kenny Leon's riveting, must-see production proves to be more than worth the wait.
It may be the most heated moment currently on any local stage. For its reflection of a case of national despair, it's not to be missed.
Director Kenny Leon's solid production for Roundabout, with an exceptional ensemble led by Blair Underwood and David Alan Grier, is the drama's first time on Broadway.
In its trim two-hour frame, “A Soldier’s Play” sees generations colliding on The Great White Way.
Underwood's oracular style is honest and spellbinding.
For the most part, 'A Soldier's Play' makes for an involving mystery saga – not unlike a particularly good episode of a television legal drama such as 'Law & Order.'
It’s a searing performance from an actor best known for his work in comedies like “In Living Color” and “The Carmichael Show.”
Leon’s direction brings out more emotional depth from the actors portraying the lower echelon soldiers than the three stars, as if they were in a different play than the leads.
Even when black people succeed in America, Fuller says, they’re still first and foremost seen by this country as black.
Kenny Leon‘s staging is mesmerizing, with soldiers in barracks singing and stamping in a bluesy march time and moving in dance steps.
By contrast, the Roundabout Theatre Company's lean, suspenseful and entertaining revival of Charles Fuller's A Soldier's Play, while it unfolds during World War II, feels quite relevant.
Cavils aside, there's enough dramatic interest, socio-historical dynamite, and charismatic energy in this revival of 'A Soldier's Play' to keep you at attention throughout its hour and 50 minutes.

cn.t: Critics praise this long-overdue Broadway debut of Fuller's Pulitzer-winning drama as still powerfully relevant, with strong performances led by David Alan Grier examining racism's corrosive impact within a WWII-era segregated Army unit.

vs.sum: Completed a major renovation in early 2026 with all seats replaced and legroom expanded, making it one of Broadway's most comfortable and modern houses. New restrooms significantly reduce intermission wait times.

acc.note: Elevators to all levels. 53 assistive listening devices. 11 wheelchair seats across Orchestra and Balcony.
